title: Korea holds at 2.50% as the chip recovery and renewed won weakness narrow the case for easing
summary: The Bank of Korea’s Monetary Policy Board unanimously retained the 2.50% Base Rate on 15 January. Its central forecasts had moved little since November, but the balance of risks had shifted. Faster semiconductor growth and unexpectedly firm activity overseas raised the upside risk to output. Won weakness threatened a renewed inflation impulse and housing prices continued to rise quickly around Seoul. The Board could support parts of the economy still under pressure without changing the economy-wide rate: it separately extended targeted temporary credit support by six months. That pairing makes the decision more informative than the unchanged headline rate alone (decision attachment and opening remarks, closing two pages).

Private consumption continued to recover, helped by consumer sentiment and government measures. Export growth remained strong despite tariffs, with semiconductors in the lead. Employment gains were concentrated in services. The governor attributed some of the weaker fourth-quarter growth rate to the comparison with a strong third quarter. Construction remained sluggish, but the Bank expected that drag to ease. These developments sustained a forecast broadly in line with November’s 1.8% growth projection for 2026. The Board described an increased probability of better growth rather than formally revising the number. Nor did stronger aggregate exports imply that construction firms, smaller borrowers or regional economies had participated equally in the recovery (attachment, domestic economy; opening remarks, domestic growth).

Inflation offered some latitude. December headline inflation edged down to 2.3% as the increase in agricultural, livestock and fisheries prices slowed, despite a faster increase in petroleum-product prices. Core inflation excluding food and energy held at 2.0%, while short-term inflation expectations among the public remained at 2.6%. These are three different measures. The November forecasts of 2.1% headline and 2.0% core inflation for 2026 remained broadly applicable. Stable global oil prices helped the projected return toward target. A persistently elevated domestic price of foreign currency could weaken that mechanism; the Board also identified government price-stabilisation measures as relevant to the path (attachment, consumer prices).

The FX market showed the limits of reading a change in one participant’s demand as a change in the overall balance. Stabilisation measures in late December had been followed by a decline of more than 40 won per dollar. Early in the new year the exchange rate again reached the mid-to-upper KRW 1,400s. The governor pointed to dollar strength, yen weakness and geopolitical developments, alongside demand from residents investing overseas. The national pension fund’s foreign investment had declined, but investment by other residents had accelerated to a pace comparable to its peak in October–November. The remarks do not allocate a share of the currency movement to each factor. They do explain why an investor observing only pension flows could have underestimated continuing pressure (opening remarks, financial markets and rationale).

Domestic credit quantities and housing prices also sent different signals. Growth in household borrowing was slowing as housing-related loan growth eased and other loans recorded net repayments. Seoul prices nevertheless continued to rise at an annualised pace of around 10%, with some spillover into nearby areas outside the regulated zones. The annualised pace is a local measure and cannot be applied to national prices or treated as a forecast for the full year. Those conditions made broad easing a competing financial-stability risk. The six-month extension of Temporary Special Support for low-credit self-employed people and SMEs concentrated assistance where the recovery was delayed (opening remarks, housing and final paragraph).

The Board also recorded a rise and subsequent partial decline in Korean Treasury yields as expectations for a Base Rate cut weakened. Korean stocks had rallied on expectations of stronger earnings, with large sector differences. Overseas, less confidence in additional rate cuts and concerns about fiscal sustainability had lifted long sovereign yields. The remarks expected divergent US and euro-area inflation trends and a moderation in Chinese growth cushioned by domestic policy. These are explanations of conditions as understood on the meeting date. Neither document gives a meeting-window price change or pre-meeting probability for the January decision. Separating the pricing of domestic policy, foreign duration and semiconductor earnings therefore requires contemporaneous market evidence beyond these releases.

questions.question: What would distinguish a durable decline in dollar demand from another temporary stabilisation?
questions.detail: The governor documents a fall in the pension fund’s foreign investment alongside a rebound in other residents’ investment. Spot FX alone cannot separate those flows from dollar and yen moves. For a won or rates position, compare available balance-of-payments and securities-flow releases by investor group with currency-hedging information. Examine how persistent the offset between pension and non-pension flows is before attributing the change to any one group.

questions.question: How far is the export improvement spreading beyond semiconductors?
questions.detail: Stronger chip exports moved the risks around the 1.8% outlook while construction and regional SMEs remained weak. Breadth matters both to the expected policy rate and to equity exposure concentrated in major exporters. Compare customs releases by product and destination with service employment, construction activity and consumption. Use the November Bank forecast as the point-in-time baseline and look for evidence of spillovers into domestic cash flow.

questions.question: Are slower household loan flows restraining Seoul housing demand where the Board sees the greatest risks?
questions.detail: The opening remarks provide a national lending trend and a local annualised price pace. They do not identify the marginal buyer or financing source in the fast-rising districts. This distinction affects the scope for a lower rate and any exposure to local lenders. Seek district-level transactions, mortgage origination by buyer type and geographic information on the regulated areas before inferring that aggregate deleveraging has contained local risk.
